blocks.text: **The problem.** Given strings `s` and `p` of lowercase letters, return the start index of every **substring** of `s` that is an anagram of `p`, in any order.

blocks.alt: s is c b a e b a b a c d, p is abc. Windows of three letters slide along s. The window at index 0, c b a, is an anagram of abc, and so is the window at index 6, b a c. The answer is 0 and 6.

blocks.text: Questions about the best or every **substring** with some property — *longest without repeats*, *shortest containing all of t*, *every window that's an anagram of p* — share one move. Keep a **window** `s[left..right]` and a summary of what's inside it (usually letter counts). Move `right` to take in a character, move `left` to let one go, and update the summary in O(1) each time. Each character enters once and leaves once, so the whole scan is O(n) instead of checking O(n²) substrings.

There are two shapes. A **fixed-size** window slides in lockstep — this lesson, where every anagram of p has exactly |p| letters. A **variable-size** window grows until something breaks and shrinks until it's fixed — the next two lessons. (The Hash Map course solves Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters this way too.)
1. Brute force: check every window from scratch
Sort each window of length |p| and compare with p sorted.

blocks.code:
def find_anagrams(s, p):
    target = sorted(p)
    m = len(p)
    return [i for i in range(len(s) - m + 1) if sorted(s[i:i + m]) == target]   # re-sort every window

blocks.text: **Time O(n · m log m), space O(m)** for n = |s| and m = |p|: every one of the n - m + 1 windows is copied and sorted. Neighbouring windows share all but two letters, and that work is thrown away.

Count p's letters once in `need`. Slide a window of exactly |p| letters over s, keeping its counts in `have`: each step adds the letter entering on the right and removes the one leaving on the left. Whenever `have` equals `need`, the window is an anagram.

blocks.caption: One letter in, one letter out per step; a window whose counts all match is an anagram.

blocks.code:
def find_anagrams(s, p):
    result = []
    m = len(p)
    if m > len(s):
        return result
    need, have = [0] * 26, [0] * 26
    for ch in p:
        need[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1
    for right in range(len(s)):
        have[ord(s[right]) - ord("a")] += 1          # the window takes in s[right]...
        left = right - m + 1
        if left < 0:
            continue                      # not full yet
        if have == need:                  # ...counts match: an anagram starts at left
            result.append(left)
        have[ord(s[left]) - ord("a")] -= 1           # ...then lets go of s[left]
    return result

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** Each step changes two counters and compares 26 — a constant. (Tracking how many of the 26 counters currently match turns the comparison into O(1) too, but 26 is already constant.)

blocks.alt: Sort every window: O(n·m log m) time, O(m) space. Sliding counts: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: **p longer than s** — no window fits: `[]`.
**Repeated letters in p** — `"aab"` needs two a's; counts handle it, a set of letters wouldn't.
**Removing in the wrong order** — check the window *before* letting go of `s[left]`; otherwise the window is one letter short.
**Permutation in String** — return `true` if *any* window is an anagram: the same loop, returning at the first match.
**Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters** — a variable window that shrinks whenever a letter repeats (Hash Map course).
**Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Length k** — a fixed window carrying one count instead of 26.
